newsitem.title: HONG KONG: WEEK AHEAD - HK stocks seen firm but rangebound.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - HK stocks seen firm but rangebound.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks are expected to trade in a narrow range with an upward bias this week ahead of the government budget and major company results, supported by positive trends on Wall Street, analysts said.
"Bonds could lead the market on a modest rally...despite signs of persistent profit-taking," said David Robinson, regional investment strategist at HSBC James Capel.

The Hang Seng Index closed 79.01 points lower at 13,337.35 on Friday, but off an intra-day of 13,304.24. During the week, the index shed 61.37 points, or 0.5 percent, on heavy turnover averaging HK$10.81 billion a day.

The U.S. bond and equity markets reacted favourably on Friday to the U.S. employment report for February which showed unemployment falling. But a weaker-than-expected rise in wages tempered fears that wage pressures would boost price inflation.

Local factors in the bull's favour in the week ahead include an uptick in residential property prices, and Wednesday's presentation of the territory's budget for fiscal 1997/98 ending March 31, which was expected to be generally positive, Robinson said.

Details released last week showed government spending will rise 6.9 percent in 1997/98, lower than the 7.6 percent increase in the 1996/97. A larger-than-forecast 1996/97 budget surplus is also expected to be announced on Wednesday.

Also, an increase in liquidity in the Chinese financial system is likely, following a coming phased reduction of Chinese banks' reserve requirement to 10 percent from the current 13 percent, which should flow through to Hong Kong markets in time, Robinson said.
Institutional interest in the market declined last week, while individual investors were again more active, trading heavily in lower priced new issues and China concept stocks.
That is because Hong Kong's blue chips were seen as slightly expensive, brokers said.
"We are now trading at about 14 times 1997 earnings (for blue chips), higher than the historic average but not the top of the range" said Robinson.
Charles Cheung at J&A Securities said: "Technically, the market still looks healthy."
The index is likely to trade in a narrower range of 13,300 to 13,600 in the coming week, he said. "All short-term technical indicators are seesawing (in neutral ranges)."

But the accumulated advance decline ratio, a good indicator of market sentiment which measures the number of rising stocks against the number of falling stocks over a time period, is still trending up, Cheung added.
The outlook for the market's key property sector is mixed.
"The capacity of stronger sales to push up prices (of property shares) is limited," said Robinson. "It has been largely discounted."
He said the government is likely to increase land supply, the shortage of which is seen as a factor for high property prices.
Key company results due this week are another factor for market direction.

Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd will report its 1996 earnings on Wednesday. The company, which is 43.86 percent owned by Swire Pacific Ltd and 25 percent owned by CITIC Pacific Ltd, is forecast to show between 24 percent and 34 percent earnings growth.
Swire Pacific, which is reporting on Friday, is forecast to report modest earnings growth of 14 percent.
